# Why the big cat puts his paws in his mouth

## Who and when

The "big cat" is **Ronald**, the enormous, pear-shaped lavender/grey cat from *Nature Cat*
(this video is a full episode; the first half is the "Wild Batts!" segment). Ronald is Nature
Cat's neighbour: a pampered, lazy indoor house cat who lives in a fancy mansion, lounges on a
velvet chaise longue under an oil painting of himself, and generally cannot be bothered with
the outdoors.

The moment in question happens at roughly **3:23–3:29 (t ≈ 203–209 seconds)** of the video.
The set-up immediately before it is this: Nature Cat, Daisy (the white rabbit), Squeeks (the
small blue mouse) and Hal (the dog) have built a wildlife-watching blind out of a big cardboard
box in the back yard and are crouched inside it at dusk, peering out through a cut-out window,
waiting to spot bats. Ronald, who had stayed behind lounging indoors, comes over to them — he
is the visitor here. He flops down on the grass right next to their box.

While Squeeks stands on the grass in front of him, pointing up at him and talking at him
continuously (Squeeks is the group's fact-explainer), Ronald **raises both front paws to his
open mouth, presses his curled toes against/into it, and holds that pose motionless for about
six seconds**, with heavy, half-lidded, thoroughly unimpressed eyes. Frame-by-frame, his mouth
is wide open with the red tongue and his teeth showing just before the paws come up, and the
same bared-teeth mouth is revealed again the instant the paws drop away. Then he lowers his
paws, closes his mouth, and sits there with a bored expression while Daisy, watching from the
box window, pulls a grimace.

## Why he does it

**He is doing what a cat does: he is licking and nibbling his own paws — grooming himself —
because he is bored and completely uninterested in what the others have invited him over to
do.** That is the point of the gag, and it works on three levels:

1. **It is literal cat behaviour.** Real cats clean themselves by putting their paws in their
   mouths, licking them and chewing between the toes. Ronald is the one character in the show
   who behaves like an ordinary house cat rather than an adventurer, so the writers give him
   ordinary house-cat business. Sitting down and washing his paws is the most "just a cat"
   thing he could possibly do.

2. **It is a piece of comic body language meaning "I am not listening."** Squeeks is standing
   right in front of him, gesturing and lecturing him about the bats they are waiting for. A
   cat who answers an enthusiastic lecture by calmly starting to groom himself is
   unmistakably signalling indifference — the animation holds the pose, unmoving, for about six
   seconds precisely so that the audience reads it as "Ronald has tuned this out." His
   half-closed, droopy eyes during and after the pose reinforce that he is bored, not engaged.

3. **It fits his role in the story.** Ronald is the sceptic and the couch potato of the group.
   He has been dragged out of a comfortable house, into a dark garden, to sit on damp grass
   next to a cardboard box and wait for bats — creatures he finds creepy. Grooming himself is
   his way of physically opting out of the activity while still technically being present, and
   it is the visual joke that separates him from Nature Cat, who is thrilled about the whole
   thing.

So the short answer: **he is not choking, eating, or hurting himself — he is a cat licking and
chewing on his paws, i.e. washing himself, and he is doing it in the middle of his friends'
nature-watching expedition to show how bored and unimpressed he is by it.**

## Other readings of the same shot, and why they are weaker

The drawing is stylised, and two other interpretations of the same pose are worth stating
explicitly:

* **Nervously chewing his claws.** His mouth is drawn with clenched, gritted teeth just before
  and just after the paws are raised, and gritted teeth in this show usually mean anxiety. The
  gang is waiting in the dark for bats, and Ronald finds bats frightening in this episode, so
  nail-biting out of nerves is a plausible reading, and it is compatible with the grooming
  reading (a cat chewing its paws can read as both). What argues against nerves being the whole
  story is his eyes: through the whole hold they are lazy and half-lidded, the show's standard
  "unimpressed" expression, not the wide, darting eyes it uses for fear.

* **Cupping his paws to his mouth to whistle or call out.** Both paws come together at an open
  mouth, which is also how a two-fingered whistle is drawn. This is weaker, because nothing in
  the scene reacts to a loud noise — nobody covers their ears, no animals are startled, and
  Squeeks just keeps calmly talking at him for the whole six seconds — and because a whistle
  would not be held as a single frozen pose for that long.

* **Covering his mouth for a yawn.** His mouth is wide open right before the paws come up and
  his eyes are droopy afterwards, which is yawn-shaped. But his fingers are curled *into* the
  mouth rather than laid flat over it, and the hold is far too long for a yawn.

All three readings point at the same underlying answer about his motivation, which is the part
that actually matters: **Ronald puts his paws in his mouth because he is a house cat who would
rather be grooming himself than birdwatching, and the gesture is the show's shorthand for his
boredom and lack of interest while his friends try to get him excited about the wildlife they
are there to see.**
